paragraphs.text: This tea comes from Alishan in Chiayi, one of the areas the trade names for [high mountain tea](taiwan-oolong:high-mountain), the name Taiwan gives to tea from gardens at about 1,000 metres and higher. The label says where the leaf grew, not which cultivar or recipe made it. At that height the plant grows slowly, and the trade traces the character of the tea to that slow growth.

The leaf was lightly oxidised, rolled in the high mountain way and given only a light roast, making it an [oolong](oolong:definition), the partly oxidised tea that stands between green and red. [Oolong came to Taiwan](taiwan-oolong:history) with settlers from Fujian, and high mountain tea rose in the late twentieth century, as more of the island's tea came to be drunk at home than sold abroad.

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: In light high mountain tea: a sweet, floral cup, often creamy or buttery, with little bitterness and a long sweet aftertaste. In roasted Dong Ding: caramel, ripe fruit, nuts and a toasted aroma. In Baozhong: floral notes and a clear, bright liquor. In Oriental Beauty: ripe fruit and honey, with little bitterness.
